exampleGross.sections: Entire tumour mapped (A1–A18): cystic duct margin (A1), adenocarcinoma-predominant areas (A2–A8), neuroendocrine-rich fleshy nodule (A9–A12), full-thickness peritoneal wall (A13–A15), hepatic-side wall (A16), remaining (A17–A18). Nodes entirely (B1–B8).

micro.text: All 8 cassettes show prostatic transition-zone tissue with nodular hyperplasia (benign prostatic hyperplasia). It is a mixed pattern of glandular and stromal nodules:

Glandular nodules: Crowded, variably dilated benign glands with papillary infoldings and undulating lumens, lined by tall columnar secretory cells with pale cytoplasm and an intact basal cell layer. Many lumens contain corpora amylacea.
Stromal nodules: Circumscribed fibromuscular and smooth-muscle nodules, some with prominent small vessels, without atypia.

Basal cell hyperplasia: Focal. Small solid and cribriform-like nests of bland basal cells, 2 or more layers thick, with ovoid nuclei, small nucleoli and scant cytoplasm. The features are typical for this benign mimic.
Chronic prostatitis: Mild chronic periglandular and stromal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation. One small focus of acute inflammation with intraluminal neutrophils. No granulomas.

Infarct with squamous metaplasia: One cassette (A5) contains a small, recent infarct of a hyperplastic nodule. At its edge the glands show reactive squamous metaplasia with mild reactive atypia. Mitoses are confined to the reactive epithelium, with no infiltrative growth.

Cautery artefact is present at chip edges and does not hinder interpretation. No high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (HGPIN), atypical small acinar proliferation, intraductal carcinoma or invasive adenocarcinoma is identified. Urothelium from the prostatic urethra is present on a few chips and is unremarkable. No bladder-neck muscle with tumour is seen.
Immunohistochemistry:

Not performed and not required. All glands have a readily identifiable basal cell layer on H&E. The basal cell hyperplasia and squamous metaplasia show classic benign features. Basal cell markers (p63, high-molecular-weight cytokeratin 34βE12 / CK5/6) and AMACR (P504S) are kept for small atypical foci that cannot be resolved on H&E. They were not needed in this case.

finalDiagnosis.label: Prostate, transurethral resection (18 g; 12 g submitted entirely):
finalDiagnosis.text: Nodular hyperplasia (benign prostatic hyperplasia), mixed glandular and stromal type. Focal basal cell hyperplasia. Mild chronic prostatitis. Small focal infarct with reactive squamous metaplasia.
Negative for high-grade PIN and carcinoma in the tissue examined.

comment.text: Incidental prostatic adenocarcinoma is found in about 5–15% of TURP specimens in published series, and is less frequent in the PSA-screening era. Most such cancers are low volume and low grade. The initial 12 g, which includes the tissue most likely to show carcinoma, was submitted entirely. Submitting this amount detects nearly all clinically significant (cT1b) incidental cancers. The remaining 6 g is kept and can be processed on request.

TURP samples mainly the transition zone. Most prostatic carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, which TURP does not usually sample. A benign TURP therefore does not exclude carcinoma elsewhere in the gland. Please correlate with serum PSA (3.4 ng/mL; PSA density about 0.07 ng/mL/cc), DRE and follow-up. Consider MRI and/or targeted biopsy if PSA rises or the DRE becomes abnormal. Note that post-TURP PSA falls because of reduced gland volume.
The infarct with squamous metaplasia and the basal cell hyperplasia are recognised benign mimics of carcinoma. They show classic features here and did not need immunohistochemistry.

containers.text: Received in formalin, labelled with the patient's name and 'TURP chips', multiple grey-white to tan, rubbery, partly cauterised prostatic chips weighing 18 g in total (blotted). Chips range from 0.3 to 1.5 cm in greatest dimension. Some show a nodular cut surface. No yellow, firm or gritty chips are seen. A small amount of blood clot is removed and not weighed.

exampleGross.sections: Initial 12 g submitted entirely in cassettes A1–A8 (about 1.5 g per cassette), as recommended in CAP guidance for TURP specimens. Includes all chips that are firm, yellow or otherwise abnormal (none seen). The remaining 6 g is kept in formalin. It would be submitted entirely if carcinoma were found in the initial cassettes, particularly in a younger patient or a candidate for curative treatment, to separate cT1a from cT1b.

micro.text: A – Antrum: antral mucosa with a dense, band-like lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate filling the lamina propria, with two lymphoid follicles with germinal centres. Neutrophils infiltrate the foveolar and surface epithelium, forming focal pit abscesses. Numerous curved, rod-shaped Helicobacter-like organisms lie in the surface mucus and along the foveolar epithelium. Glands are preserved (no atrophy). No intestinal metaplasia.
B – Incisura: antral-type mucosa with moderate chronic inflammation, mild neutrophilic activity and scanty organisms. No atrophy or intestinal metaplasia.
C – Corpus: oxyntic mucosa with mild superficial chronic inflammation, minimal activity and scanty organisms. Oxyntic glands preserved.
No dysplasia, lymphoepithelial lesions, or atypical lymphoid infiltrate suggestive of MALT lymphoma.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Giemsa (A, B, C): Helicobacter-like organisms present: numerous in A, scanty in B and C

finalDiagnosis.label: A–C. Stomach, antrum, incisura and corpus, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Chronic active gastritis, antrum-predominant, with lymphoid follicles, associated with Helicobacter pylori (Giemsa positive).
No atrophy or intestinal metaplasia (OLGA 0, OLGIM 0). No dysplasia or lymphoma.

comment.text: The features are typical of active Helicobacter pylori infection. The gastritis is non-atrophic and antrum-predominant, a pattern associated with duodenal ulcer disease. Lymphoid follicles are characteristic of H. pylori infection and explain the nodular endoscopic appearance.

Eradication therapy is recommended per guidelines (choice guided by local resistance patterns), with confirmation of eradication by urea breath test or stool antigen at least 4 weeks after therapy and 2 weeks off PPI.

Incisura: One tan mucosal fragment, 3 mm. Embedded entirely (B1).

diagnoses.name: Multifocal Atrophic Gastritis with Intestinal Metaplasia (OLGA III, OLGIM II)

micro.text: A – Antrum: antral mucosa with loss of antral glands (about 50% of gland area) and moderate replacement by intestinal metaplasia. The metaplasia has goblet cells and absorptive cells, and is predominantly complete type (brush border, Paneth cells present), with focal incomplete type. Moderate chronic inflammation and mild neutrophilic activity. Scanty Helicobacter-like organisms on the remaining non-metaplastic foveolar epithelium.
B – Incisura: similar changes, with moderate atrophy and moderate intestinal metaplasia (the incisura is scored with the antrum for OLGA/OLGIM).

C – Corpus: oxyntic mucosa with moderate loss of oxyntic glands (about 40%), with pseudopyloric (spasmolytic polypeptide-expressing) metaplasia and mild focal intestinal metaplasia. Mild chronic inflammation. Activity absent. No organisms identified.
No dysplasia in any biopsy. No malignancy.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Giemsa (A, B, C): Scanty Helicobacter-like organisms in A
H. pylori immunohistochemistry (A, B, C): Positive, scanty, in A; negative in B and C
Alcian blue / PAS (pH 2.5): Confirms goblet cells (IM); sialomucin-rich focal incomplete-type IM in A

finalDiagnosis.label: A–C. Stomach, antrum, incisura and corpus, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Chronic multifocal atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia, associated with Helicobacter pylori (scanty, antrum).
OLGA stage III; OLGIM stage II (high-risk OLGA stage). Negative for dysplasia.

comment.text: Multifocal atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia is the long-term result of H. pylori infection and lies on the Correa pathway to intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma. OLGA stage III–IV is regarded as high risk. Organisms are scanty because atrophy and metaplasia make the mucosa less hospitable to them. A negative stain on metaplastic mucosa does not exclude infection, so serology or a breath test is advised.

Management per MAPS II (2019) and the BSG 2019 guidance: H. pylori eradication, and endoscopic surveillance with high-quality endoscopy about every 3 years for advanced stages (OLGA/OLGIM III–IV), with a shorter interval if there is a family history of gastric cancer (as here) or incomplete IM. Follow local protocol.

containers.text: Antrum: Two tan mucosal fragments, 3–4 mm. Embedded entirely (A1).
Incisura: One fragment, 3 mm. Embedded entirely (B1).
Corpus: Two fragments, 3 mm each. Embedded entirely (C1).

micro.text: A, B – Antrum: ulcerated antral mucosa with granulation tissue, fibrinopurulent exudate and mixed inflammation. In the ulcer base (B) and the adjacent lamina propria, many enlarged endothelial and stromal cells, and occasional glandular epithelial cells, contain large amphophilic intranuclear inclusions with a perinuclear halo (owl’s-eye) and granular cytoplasmic inclusions. These are characteristic of cytomegalovirus. Apoptotic bodies are present in the glands, with mild neutrophilic cryptitis-like gland injury. No vasculitis.
C – Corpus: mild chronic inflammation with occasional CMV-infected cells, confirmed on immunohistochemistry.

No Helicobacter-like organisms. No fungal or herpes simplex virus (HSV) inclusions. No post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD)-type atypical lymphoid infiltrate. No dysplasia or malignancy.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
CMV immunohistochemistry (A, B, C): Positive nuclear staining. Inclusion-bearing cells: about 25 per tissue fragment in B, 6 in A and 3 in C
HSV-1/2 immunohistochemistry (B): Negative
EBER in situ hybridisation (B): Negative (no evidence of EBV-related PTLD)
Giemsa (A–C): No Helicobacter-like organisms
Grocott (GMS) (B): No fungi

finalDiagnosis.label: A–C. Stomach, antrum (ulcer edge and base) and corpus, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) gastritis with ulceration. Characteristic inclusions confirmed by CMV immunohistochemistry.
No HSV, fungi or PTLD. Helicobacter pylori not identified. No dysplasia or malignancy.

comment.text: The findings confirm tissue-invasive CMV disease of the stomach in an immunosuppressed transplant recipient. CMV infects endothelial and stromal cells most often, so the ulcer base is the highest-yield biopsy site.

CMV immunohistochemistry is more sensitive than H&E and is recommended when the index of suspicion is high, even if no inclusions are seen. Please notify the transplant team urgently for antiviral therapy and adjustment of immunosuppression. The updated Sydney System is not applicable.

containers.text: Antrum ulcer edge: Three fragments. Embedded entirely (A1).
Antrum ulcer base: Two fragments. Embedded entirely (B1).
Corpus: Two fragments. Embedded entirely (C1).

diagnoses.name: Autoimmune Atrophic Gastritis with ECL-cell Hyperplasia

micro.text: A – Antrum: antral mucosa with preserved glands, mild superficial chronic inflammation and no activity. Mild foveolar hyperplasia. Chromogranin and gastrin immunohistochemistry show G-cell hyperplasia (secondary to hypochlorhydria).
B – Incisura: antral-type mucosa within normal limits apart from mild chronic inflammation.

C – Corpus: there is marked loss of oxyntic glands with near-complete loss of parietal and chief cells. These are replaced by pseudopyloric (antralised) glands and moderate intestinal metaplasia (complete type), with focal pancreatic acinar metaplasia. The lamina propria has moderate lymphoplasmacytic inflammation that is deep, around the glands, with focal destruction of residual oxyntic glands and scattered eosinophils. Chromogranin immunohistochemistry shows enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cell hyperplasia: linear chains (5 or more cells in a row, at least 2 per mm of mucosa) and micronodular clusters (5 or more cells, 30–150 µm). There is no adenomatoid hyperplasia, dysplasia (more than 150 µm) or neuroendocrine tumour.
D – Corpus polyp: oxyntic-type mucosa with hyperplastic foveolae and residual oxyntic glands (pseudopolyp of residual oxyntic mucosa). No dysplasia and no NET.
No Helicobacter-like organisms (Giemsa and immunohistochemistry). No dysplasia or malignancy.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Chromogranin A (A, C, D): C: linear and micronodular ECL-cell hyperplasia. A: increased G cells. D: no NET
Gastrin (A): G-cell hyperplasia in the antrum
Synaptophysin (C): Confirms the neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
Giemsa and H. pylori immunohistochemistry (A–C): Negative

finalDiagnosis.label: A, B. Stomach, antrum and incisura, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Antral mucosa with mild chronic gastritis and G-cell hyperplasia. No atrophy.

finalDiagnosis.label: C. Stomach, corpus, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Autoimmune atrophic gastritis (corpus-restricted, marked atrophy) with pseudopyloric and intestinal metaplasia, and linear and micronodular ECL-cell hyperplasia.

finalDiagnosis.label: D. Stomach, corpus polyp, polypectomy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Pseudopolyp of residual oxyntic mucosa with foveolar hyperplasia. No dysplasia or neuroendocrine tumour.
OLGA stage II; OLGIM stage II. Helicobacter pylori not identified. No dysplasia or neuroendocrine tumour.

comment.text: The corpus-restricted atrophy with antral sparing and antral G-cell hyperplasia, together with anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, hypergastrinaemia and B12 deficiency, confirm autoimmune atrophic gastritis with pernicious anaemia.

Hypergastrinaemia drives ECL-cell hyperplasia. The sequence is linear, then micronodular, then adenomatoid hyperplasia, then dysplasia, and finally type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumour. Patients also have an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.
OLGA/OLGIM were designed for H. pylori gastritis. In autoimmune gastritis they underestimate the corpus-predominant disease, so they are given for completeness only.

Follow-up per guidelines (for example AGA 2021 clinical practice update): endoscopic surveillance, often every 3 years, adjusted to the individual's risk, with corpus mapping biopsies and removal of polyps. Also check B12, iron and thyroid status.

containers.text: Antrum: Two tan fragments, 3 mm. Embedded entirely (A1).
Incisura: One fragment, 3 mm. Embedded entirely (B1).
Corpus: Two fragments, 2–3 mm. Embedded entirely (C1).
Corpus polyp: One sessile polypoid fragment, 4 mm. Embedded entirely (D1).

diagnoses.name: Acute Erosive and Haemorrhagic Gastropathy, NSAID-associated

micro.text: A – Antrum: antral mucosa with superficial erosions. These show loss of the surface epithelium with overlying fibrin, a little neutrophilic debris, and haemorrhage into the superficial lamina propria. Lamina propria oedema and congestion. Adjacent foveolae show reactive regenerative changes: mucin depletion, nuclear enlargement with small nucleoli, and increased mitoses confined to the neck zone. Inflammation is sparse, with no significant chronic gastritis.
B – Corpus: oxyntic mucosa with focal subepithelial haemorrhage and mild oedema. Otherwise unremarkable.
No Helicobacter-like organisms on H&E or Giemsa. No dysplasia, granulomas, viral inclusions or malignancy.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Giemsa (A, B): No Helicobacter-like organisms

finalDiagnosis.label: A. Stomach, antrum, biopsy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Acute erosive and haemorrhagic gastropathy with reactive epithelial changes, compatible with NSAID injury in this clinical setting.

finalDiagnosis.label: B. Stomach, corpus, biopsy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Oxyntic mucosa with focal superficial haemorrhage. No significant gastritis.
Helicobacter pylori not identified (H&E and Giemsa). No dysplasia or malignancy.

comment.text: The features are those of an acute erosive / haemorrhagic gastropathy. Inflammation is minimal, so this is a gastropathy rather than a gastritis. With the clinical history, NSAID injury is the most likely cause. Similar changes occur with alcohol, aspirin, stress (critical illness) and ischaemia. The reactive epithelial atypia is confined to the regenerative zone, with surface maturation, and is not dysplasia.
The updated Sydney synoptic is not applied here because there is no gastritis to grade.

containers.text: Antrum: Three tan, partly haemorrhagic mucosal fragments, 2–3 mm. All embedded (A1).
Corpus: Two tan mucosal fragments, 2–3 mm. All embedded (B1).

micro.text: A – Antrum: antral mucosa with features of chemical (reactive) gastropathy:
Foveolae: Foveolar hyperplasia with elongated, tortuous, corkscrew-like pits. Mucin depletion and reactive nuclear enlargement of the foveolar epithelium.
Lamina propria: Oedema, vascular congestion and ectasia. Smooth-muscle fibres extend upward between the foveolae.
Inflammation: Sparse; no neutrophilic activity.
B – Corpus: oxyntic mucosa within normal limits.
No Helicobacter-like organisms. No atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia or malignancy.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Giemsa (A, B): No Helicobacter-like organisms

finalDiagnosis.label: A. Stomach, antrum, biopsy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Chemical (reactive) gastropathy, compatible with bile reflux in this clinical setting.

finalDiagnosis.label: B. Stomach, corpus, biopsy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Oxyntic mucosa within normal limits.
Helicobacter pylori not identified (Giemsa). No dysplasia or malignancy.

comment.text: Chemical (reactive) gastropathy is caused by duodenogastric (bile) reflux, NSAIDs, alcohol and other chemical irritants. It shows epithelial and vascular changes with little inflammation, so it is not graded by the updated Sydney System.
The reactive nuclear changes mature towards the surface and should not be mistaken for dysplasia.

containers.text: Antrum: Three tan fragments, 2–4 mm. Embedded entirely (A1).
Corpus: Two tan fragments, 3 mm. Embedded entirely (B1).

micro.text: A, B – Stomach: antral and oxyntic mucosa (corpus more involved) with marked intraepithelial lymphocytosis of the surface and foveolar epithelium. CD3 counts: 42 per 100 epithelial cells in the corpus and 31 per 100 in the antrum (threshold 25 or more). There is a mild to moderate lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the lamina propria, with focal erosion in B. Activity is minimal. No Helicobacter-like organisms. No atrophy or intestinal metaplasia.

C – Duodenum: subtotal villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (about 70 per 100 enterocytes), with a lymphoplasmacytic lamina propria. These features are Marsh–Oberhuber type 3b.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
CD3 (A, B, C): Highlights increased intraepithelial T lymphocytes (counts above)
Giemsa (A, B): No Helicobacter-like organisms

finalDiagnosis.label: A, B. Stomach, antrum and corpus, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Lymphocytic gastritis (corpus-predominant).

finalDiagnosis.label: C. Duodenum, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Duodenal mucosa with subtotal villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Marsh–Oberhuber 3b), consistent with coeliac disease with positive serology.
Helicobacter pylori not identified (Giemsa). No dysplasia or malignancy.

comment.text: Lymphocytic gastritis is defined by 25 or more intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 surface and foveolar epithelial cells. The most common associations are coeliac disease (about 1/3 of cases or more in some series) and H. pylori infection. Others include Crohn disease, drugs, lymphocytic or collagenous colitis, Ménétrier-like changes, and HIV. Lymphocytic gastritis is found in about 10–45% of untreated coeliac patients.
A gluten-free diet usually improves both the gastric and the duodenal changes. The updated Sydney System is not used for this pattern; the key counts are summarised instead.

containers.text: Antrum: Two tan fragments, 3 mm. Embedded entirely (A1).
Corpus: Two fragments, 3 mm. Embedded entirely (B1).
Duodenum: Five fragments, 2–4 mm, orientated on filter paper. Embedded entirely (C1–C2).

micro.text: B – Corpus: oxyntic mucosa with an irregular, thickened subepithelial collagen band up to 45 µm (normal less than 10 µm). The band contains entrapped capillaries and inflammatory cells, and its lower edge is ragged. The surface epithelium is damaged and focally detached from the band. The lamina propria contains a moderately dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with increased eosinophils (up to 25 per HPF). Glands are focally reduced in the depressed areas.
A – Antrum: a patchy, thinner collagen band (up to 15 µm) with mild chronic inflammation.
C – Duodenum: normal villous architecture. No increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes. No subepithelial collagen.
No Helicobacter-like organisms. No dysplasia or malignancy.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Masson trichrome (A, B): Highlights the thickened subepithelial collagen band (blue)
Tenascin immunohistochemistry (B): Strong subepithelial band staining, supporting collagenous gastritis
Giemsa (A, B): No Helicobacter-like organisms

finalDiagnosis.label: A, B. Stomach, antrum and corpus, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Collagenous gastritis (corpus-predominant). Subepithelial collagen band up to 45 µm, confirmed on Masson trichrome and tenascin.

finalDiagnosis.label: C. Duodenum, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: No significant pathology. No collagenous sprue.
Helicobacter pylori not identified (Giemsa). No dysplasia or malignancy.

comment.text: Collagenous gastritis is rare. The paediatric / young-adult form, as here, is usually limited to the stomach. It causes anaemia and abdominal pain, with a nodular corpus at endoscopy: the nodules are relatively spared mucosa between atrophic depressed areas. The adult form is often associated with collagenous colitis or sprue, coeliac disease, or autoimmune disorders.
Biopsies from both the nodules and the depressed areas improve diagnostic yield. Treatment is empirical (PPI, iron, sometimes budesonide).

containers.text: Antrum: Two tan fragments, 3 mm. Embedded entirely (A1).
Corpus: Four fragments, 2–4 mm, from nodules and the depressed areas between them. Embedded entirely (B1–B2).
Duodenum: Four fragments. Embedded entirely (C1).

micro.text: A–C – Stomach: dense lamina propria eosinophilic infiltrate. It is most marked in the antrum, where eosinophils form sheets and infiltrate the foveolar epithelium and muscularis mucosae, with eosinophilic gland abscesses and degranulation. There is reactive epithelial change and mild chronic inflammation, with no neutrophilic activity.
D – Duodenum: normal villous architecture. Eosinophils up to 22 per HPF (within normal limits).
No parasites, Helicobacter-like organisms, granulomas, vasculitis, mast-cell aggregates, or atypical lymphoid infiltrate. No dysplasia.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Giemsa (A–C): No Helicobacter-like organisms
CD117 / tryptase (A): No mast-cell aggregates (systemic mastocytosis not suggested)

finalDiagnosis.label: A–C. Stomach, antrum, incisura and corpus, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Marked mucosal eosinophilia (peak 112 per HPF; 30 or more per HPF in at least 5 HPF in both antrum and corpus) with intraepithelial eosinophils and eosinophilic gland abscesses. Consistent with eosinophilic gastritis in the appropriate clinical context.

finalDiagnosis.label: D. Duodenum, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: No significant eosinophilia (no eosinophilic duodenitis).
Helicobacter pylori not identified (Giemsa). No dysplasia or malignancy.

comment.text: The counts exceed commonly used thresholds for eosinophilic gastritis: 30 or more eosinophils per HPF in at least 5 HPF (Lwin et al. 2011), with supportive features such as intraepithelial eosinophils, gland abscesses and muscularis mucosae infiltration. Normal gastric eosinophil counts vary by geography and site, so state the method (HPF area) used.

Before a diagnosis of primary eosinophilic gastritis, exclude secondary causes: parasites (Anisakis, Strongyloides), drug reaction, H. pylori, inflammatory bowel disease, connective tissue disease or vasculitis (EGPA), hypereosinophilic syndrome, and mastocytosis. Correlate clinically. The updated Sydney System is not used for this pattern.

containers.text: Antrum: Two fragments. Embedded entirely (A1).
Incisura: One fragment. Embedded entirely (B1).
Corpus: Two fragments. Embedded entirely (C1).
Duodenum: Four fragments. Embedded entirely (D1).

micro.text: A – Antrum: antral mucosa with patchy chronic active inflammation. Two compact, well-formed, non-necrotising epithelioid granulomas lie in the lamina propria, one next to a gland with focal cryptitis. There are focal perifoveolar collections of lymphocytes and histiocytes with neutrophils (focally enhanced gastritis) and a small aphthous erosion. The intervening mucosa is relatively normal.
B – Incisura: one small non-necrotising granuloma and focally enhanced gastritis.
C – Corpus: within normal limits.
D – Duodenum: focal active duodenitis with a small epithelioid granuloma. Villous architecture is preserved.
No caseation, foreign material, fungi, acid-fast bacilli or Helicobacter-like organisms. No vasculitis. No dysplasia.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Ziehl–Neelsen (A, D): No acid-fast bacilli
Grocott (GMS) / PAS (A): No fungi
Giemsa (A–C): No Helicobacter-like organisms
Polarised light: No foreign material

finalDiagnosis.label: A, B. Stomach, antrum and incisura, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Granulomatous gastritis (non-necrotising epithelioid granulomas) with focally enhanced gastritis and aphthous erosion. Consistent with gastric involvement by Crohn disease in this clinical setting.

finalDiagnosis.label: C. Stomach, corpus, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Within normal limits.

finalDiagnosis.label: D. Duodenum, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Focal active duodenitis with a non-necrotising granuloma, consistent with Crohn disease.
No organisms on special stains. No dysplasia or malignancy.

comment.text: Gastric granulomas are found in a minority of Crohn patients, but are more frequent in children and young adults. Focally enhanced gastritis in an H. pylori-negative patient also supports Crohn disease.

Differential diagnosis of granulomatous gastritis: H. pylori infection (rarely granulomatous), tuberculosis and fungal infection (stains negative here), sarcoidosis, foreign-body or food granulomas, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a reaction to a neoplasm or lymphoma, and isolated (idiopathic) granulomatous gastritis, which is a diagnosis of exclusion. The updated Sydney System is not used for granulomatous gastritis.

containers.text: Antrum: Three fragments. Embedded entirely (A1, three levels).
Incisura: One fragment. Embedded entirely (B1, three levels).
Corpus: Two fragments. Embedded entirely (C1).
Duodenum: Four fragments. Embedded entirely (D1).

micro.text: A – Antrum: largely normal antral mucosa containing two discrete foci of perifoveolar and periglandular inflammation. These foci consist of small aggregates of lymphocytes, histiocytes and a few neutrophils around single foveolae or glands, with focal neutrophils within the epithelium. The surrounding mucosa shows no diffuse chronic inflammation.
B – Corpus: within normal limits.
No granulomas on three levels. No Helicobacter-like organisms (Giemsa and immunohistochemistry). No atrophy, intestinal metaplasia or dysplasia.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Giemsa / H. pylori immunohistochemistry (A, B): Negative
CD68 (A): Highlights histiocytes within the focal aggregates

finalDiagnosis.label: A. Stomach, antrum, biopsy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Focally enhanced gastritis (H. pylori negative). No granulomas.

finalDiagnosis.label: B. Stomach, corpus, biopsy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Within normal limits.
Helicobacter pylori not identified (Giemsa). No dysplasia or malignancy.

comment.text: Focally enhanced gastritis means focal perifoveolar or periglandular inflammation in an otherwise normal, H. pylori-negative stomach. It is reported in about 40–75% of children with Crohn disease, but it is not specific: it also occurs in ulcerative colitis, and in non-IBD patients (for example CMV, drugs, chronic granulomatous disease).

In this clinical context it supports a diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease, favouring Crohn disease. Correlate with the ileocolonoscopy biopsies (pending). The updated Sydney System is not appropriate for this focal pattern.

containers.text: Antrum: Two fragments. Embedded entirely (A1, three levels).
Corpus: Two fragments. Embedded entirely (B1).

micro.text: A, B – Corpus: markedly thickened mucosa (up to 5 mm) with massive foveolar hyperplasia. The foveolae are elongated, tortuous (corkscrew) and cystically dilated, and occupy more than half of the mucosal thickness. Some cysts extend down to and through the muscularis mucosae. The oxyntic glands are reduced, with marked loss of parietal and chief cells (oxyntic atrophy). The lamina propria shows oedema, thin strands of smooth muscle between the foveolae, and only mild lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with scattered eosinophils. Intraepithelial lymphocytes are not increased.
C – Antrum: antral mucosa within normal limits (antral sparing).
No parietal-cell hyperplasia (against Zollinger–Ellison). No dysplasia. No atypical lymphoid infiltrate or signet-ring cells. No CMV inclusions. No Helicobacter-like organisms.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
CMV immunohistochemistry (A): Negative
Giemsa / H. pylori immunohistochemistry (A–C): Negative
Cytokeratin AE1/AE3 (A): No infiltrating single cells or signet-ring cells
CD20 / CD3 (A): Mixed reactive lymphoid population; no lymphoma
H+/K+ ATPase (A): Marked reduction in parietal cells

finalDiagnosis.label: A, B. Stomach, corpus, snare and standard biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Hypertrophic gastropathy with massive foveolar hyperplasia, cystic change and oxyntic gland atrophy, with minimal inflammation. In the clinical context (giant corpus folds with antral sparing, protein-losing gastropathy, hypochlorhydria), consistent with Ménétrier disease.

finalDiagnosis.label: C. Stomach, antrum, biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Within normal limits.
No lymphoma, carcinoma, CMV or Helicobacter pylori. No dysplasia.

comment.text: Ménétrier disease is a rare acquired hypertrophic gastropathy caused by excess TGF-alpha signalling through EGFR. It shows massive foveolar hyperplasia with oxyntic atrophy and spares the antrum. It causes protein-losing gastropathy and hypochlorhydria. Standard biopsies are often too superficial to diagnose it, so a snare or full-thickness mucosal biopsy is preferred, as here.

Differential diagnoses of giant gastric folds: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (parietal-cell hyperplasia, hyperchlorhydria), lymphoma, diffuse-type carcinoma, CMV-associated Ménétrier-like disease (in children), lymphocytic gastritis, and hyperplastic or juvenile polyposis.

There is a reported increased risk of gastric carcinoma, so surveillance is advised. Anti-EGFR therapy (cetuximab) or gastrectomy are options for severe disease. The updated Sydney System is not used.

containers.text: Corpus fold, snare biopsy: One polypoid fragment of full-thickness mucosa with some submucosa, 1.8 x 1.2 x 0.6 cm. The cut surface shows thickened mucosa (up to 5 mm) with small mucoid cysts. Serially sliced and embedded entirely (A1–A3).
Corpus: Three fragments, 3–4 mm. Embedded entirely (B1).
Antrum: Two fragments, 3 mm. Embedded entirely (C1).

micro.text: Sections show a well-circumscribed lesion enclosed by a thin fibrous capsule, composed of lobules of mature univacuolated adipocytes separated by delicate fibrous septa carrying thin-walled capillaries. The adipocytes are uniform in size with small, eccentric, flattened nuclei. There are no lipoblasts, no atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells, no thickened atypical fibrous septa, and no increased vascularity, fat necrosis or mitotic activity. Capsule is intact.

finalDiagnosis.label: Subcutaneous swelling, upper back, excision:
finalDiagnosis.text: Lipoma (conventional), completely excised. No atypia or malignancy.

comment.text: Features are those of a benign adipocytic tumour (WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours). MDM2 FISH is not required for a superficial lesion of this size without atypia.

containers.text: Received a single encapsulated, lobulated, yellow fatty mass measuring 6.5 x 5.0 x 2.5 cm and weighing 38 g. The external surface is smooth with a thin, intact capsule. Cut section shows uniform, soft, greasy, yellow lobulated adipose tissue with thin fibrous septa. No haemorrhage, necrosis, firm or myxoid areas are seen.

exampleGross.sections: A1-A4: representative sections including capsule.

diagnoses.name: Chronic Tonsillitis with Reactive Follicular Hyperplasia (Tonsillectomy)

micro.text: Sections from both tonsils show surface stratified squamous epithelium with deep, branching crypts. The crypts are dilated and contain keratin debris, desquamated cells, neutrophils and bacterial colonies, including Actinomyces-like colonies. The lymphoid tissue shows marked follicular hyperplasia with prominent germinal centres with tingible-body macrophages. Interfollicular areas show fibrosis with plasma cells. Focal crypt epithelial reticulation with intraepithelial lymphocytes is seen. No granulomas, dysplasia, atypical lymphoid infiltrate or malignancy are identified.

finalDiagnosis.label: Right and left palatine tonsils, tonsillectomy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Chronic tonsillitis with reactive lymphoid follicular hyperplasia and crypt colonisation by Actinomyces-like organisms. No dysplasia or malignancy.

comment.text: Actinomyces-like colonies within tonsillar crypts are a common commensal finding and do not indicate actinomycosis in the absence of tissue invasion.

containers.text: Received two separately labelled tonsils. Right tonsil: 2.8 x 2.0 x 1.4 cm, with a tan, nodular mucosal surface and deep crypts; cut section is tan-grey with yellow cheesy material within the crypts. No discrete mass or ulceration.
Left tonsil: 3.0 x 2.1 x 1.5 cm, with a tan, nodular mucosal surface and deep crypts; cut section is tan-grey with yellow cheesy material within the crypts. No discrete mass or ulceration.

exampleGross.sections: A1-A2 right tonsil; B1-B2 left tonsil.

diagnoses.name: Tubulovillous Adenoma with Low-grade Dysplasia, Sigmoid Colon (Polypectomy)

micro.text: Sections show a colorectal adenoma with a mixed tubular and villous architecture. The villous component (finger-like fronds more than twice the height of the normal mucosa) makes up about 40% of the polyp. The tubular component forms the rest. The epithelium shows low-grade dysplasia: elongated, pencillate, pseudostratified, hyperchromatic nuclei that keep their basal polarity, with reduced mucin and preserved gland architecture. There is no complex cribriforming or back-to-back architecture, no loss of polarity, and no open vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli (no high-grade dysplasia).

The stalk is composed of normal mucosa and submucosa with a central vessel. It is free of adenoma, and the adenoma lies 2.5 mm from the inked stalk resection margin. The muscularis mucosae is intact throughout, with no submucosal invasion. Misplaced (pseudoinvasive) epithelium is absent. No lymphovascular structures contain tumour.
No serrated features (no sessile serrated lesion component). No carcinoma.

finalDiagnosis.label: A. Sigmoid colon polyp (14 mm), cold snare polypectomy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Tubulovillous adenoma (villous component about 40%) with low-grade dysplasia. Completely excised; stalk margin clear (2.5 mm). No high-grade dysplasia or invasive malignancy.

comment.text: This is an advanced adenoma because of its size (10 mm or more) and villous architecture. It is completely excised, with no high-grade dysplasia and no invasion.

Surveillance should follow current national and society guidance (BSG, ESGE or US Multi-Society Task Force). These generally base the interval on the number, size and histology of all the adenomas found at this colonoscopy, including the separately reported rectal polyps. In general terms, a single completely excised adenoma of 10 mm or more, or one with high-grade dysplasia, is a risk feature for which a surveillance colonoscopy is usually recommended, provided the baseline colonoscopy was complete and of good quality. Please apply local programme criteria.

containers.text: Sigmoid polyp: A lobulated tan polyp, 14 x 11 x 9 mm, on a short stalk 3 mm long and 4 mm wide. The stalk resection margin (diathermy-free, cold snare) is inked black. The polyp was bisected through the stalk.

exampleGross.sections: A1 central sections with the stalk; A2 lateral portions (entirely embedded). Three levels cut on A1 to assess the stalk.

micro.text: Sections show a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma composed of irregular, cribriform and fused glands lined by stratified columnar cells with pleomorphic, vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli, with luminal 'dirty' necrosis. Glands form >50% of the tumour. The tumour invades through the muscularis propria into pericolorectal adipose tissue but does not reach the serosal surface. Lymphovascular invasion is present (small vessel); no extramural venous invasion or perineural invasion. Tumour budding is low (BD1, 3 buds per 0.785 mm2). An adjacent tubulovillous adenoma remnant is noted. Two of seventeen lymph nodes show metastatic adenocarcinoma (largest deposit 6 mm, no extranodal extension). No tumour deposits. All margins are free. Appendix and terminal ileum are unremarkable.

finalDiagnosis.label: Right hemicolectomy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon, low grade (moderately differentiated), 4.5 cm, invading pericolorectal tissue, with lymphovascular invasion. Margins negative. Metastatic carcinoma in 2 of 17 lymph nodes. pT3 pN1b (AJCC 8th edition).

comment.text: Mismatch repair protein immunohistochemistry is recommended for Lynch syndrome screening and therapy planning.

containers.text: Received a right hemicolectomy specimen comprising terminal ileum 8 cm, caecum and ascending colon 18 cm, with appendix 6 cm and attached mesentery. In the ascending colon, 6 cm from the ileocaecal valve, there is an ulceroproliferative tumour measuring 4.5 x 4.0 x 1.5 cm, involving 70% of the circumference. On cut section, the grey-white tumour extends through the muscularis propria into pericolic fat. Distance to proximal margin 14 cm, distal margin 12 cm, radial (mesenteric) margin 3.0 cm. No perforation. Seventeen lymph nodes are identified (largest 1.2 cm).

exampleGross.sections: A1 proximal margin; A2 distal margin; A3-A8 tumour including deepest invasion and serosa; A9 mesenteric margin; A10 appendix; A11-A17 lymph nodes.

micro.text: The dermis contains multiple variably sized, well-circumscribed deposits of amorphous, basophilic, granular to fractured calcified material. Some deposits are surrounded by foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, histiocytes and fibrosis, and some lie free in the dermis without a reaction. Several deposits are rimmed by a thin layer of flattened cells. Focally, there is a residual keratinising squamous lining with a granular layer, one of which encloses calcified keratinous debris (an epidermal inclusion cyst remnant). Most deposits show no epithelial lining.

The overlying epidermis is unremarkable. Focal transepidermal elimination of calcium is present in A2. No needle-shaped crystals or tophaceous material. Polarisation shows no urate or foreign material. No ossification. No calcified vessels. No pilomatrical shadow cells. No malignancy. Margins are clear of the nodules.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
von Kossa: Black staining of deposits (calcium salts / phosphate)
Alizarin red S: Orange-red staining (calcium)
Polarised light: No birefringent urate crystals or foreign material
Pancytokeratin (A2, A5): Highlights residual squamous lining in a minority of nodules

finalDiagnosis.label: A. Scrotal skin with nodules, excision:
finalDiagnosis.text: Scrotal calcinosis (idiopathic calcinosis cutis of the scrotum). Multiple dermal calcified deposits, von Kossa and Alizarin red positive, with a foreign-body giant cell reaction. Focal remnants of epidermal inclusion cyst lining. Margins clear. No malignancy.

comment.text: Scrotal calcinosis presents as multiple calcified dermal nodules in men with normal calcium and phosphate metabolism. It is classified as idiopathic calcinosis cutis. Its pathogenesis is debated. Many authors regard most cases as dystrophic calcification of pre-existing epidermal inclusion (epidermoid) cysts, or of degenerated eccrine duct milia, whose linings are later destroyed by the foreign-body reaction. That would make many cases secondary rather than truly idiopathic. Others have found no cyst remnants despite step sections. The partial squamous lining in some nodules here supports the cystic origin theory for at least part of the lesion.
Differential diagnoses:
Dystrophic calcinosis: Calcium deposited in damaged tissue (connective tissue disease, trauma, tumours).
Metastatic calcinosis: Abnormal calcium or phosphate, for example in renal failure or hyperparathyroidism. Excluded by normal biochemistry.
Calcified epidermoid cyst: A single lining-preserved cyst.
Gouty tophus: Amorphous, needle-cleft material with negatively birefringent urate crystals. Absent here, with normal uric acid.
Other: Pilomatricoma (shadow cells) and calcified onchocercoma or other parasitic nodule.
Recurrence after excision is possible, as new nodules may form.

containers.text: Scrotal skin: An ellipse of rugose, pigmented skin, 5.5 x 3.0 cm, excised to a depth of 1.2 cm, with dartos muscle at the base. The skin surface carries 9 firm, white-yellow nodules, 2–9 mm. On slicing, the nodules are gritty, chalky and white. They sit in the dermis and leave a clefted cut surface. No cyst lining or keratinous contents are obvious. The deep and peripheral margins are inked.

exampleGross.sections: A1–A6 representative nodules with overlying skin and deep margin (A3 and A4 decalcified briefly, after an undecalcified block was kept for von Kossa and Alizarin red).

micro.text: A – Endobronchial biopsies: the bronchial mucosa, with respiratory epithelium at the surface, is infiltrated and focally ulcerated by an adenocarcinoma. The tumour forms crowded, back-to-back and cribriform glands with a desmoplastic, inflamed stroma.

Tumour cells: Columnar, with elongated, pseudostratified, hyperchromatic, cigar-shaped nuclei and scant, mucin-depleted eosinophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm. Conspicuous apical (luminal) mitoses and many apoptotic bodies are seen at low power. This is the morphology of usual-type HPV-associated endocervical adenocarcinoma.
Necrosis: Focal intraluminal necrotic debris.

B – Transbronchial biopsies: alveolated lung parenchyma infiltrated by the same adenocarcinoma. There is no lepidic growth along alveolar walls and no in situ (adenocarcinoma in situ-like) component. The background lung shows mild reactive changes.
No squamous or neuroendocrine component. No signet-ring cells or intracytoplasmic mucin pools (mucicarmine stain shows only focal luminal mucin).
The morphology was compared with the patient’s previous cervical biopsy slides, which were retrieved from the archive. The tumour is morphologically similar.
Immunohistochemistry / In Situ Hybridisation:
p16: Diffuse, strong, block-type nuclear and cytoplasmic positivity
High-risk HPV RNA in situ hybridisation (E6/E7 mRNA): Positive: dot-like nuclear and cytoplasmic signals in tumour cells; negative in background lung and bronchial epithelium
CK7: Diffusely positive
CEA (monoclonal): Positive (luminal and cytoplasmic)
PAX8: Negative (some HPV-associated endocervical adenocarcinomas are positive)
TTF-1 (clone SPT24 or 8G7G3/1): Negative in tumour; positive in entrapped pneumocytes (internal control)
Napsin A: Negative in tumour; positive in alveolar macrophages and pneumocytes
CK20: Negative
CDX2: Focal, weak (fewer than 5% of cells)
ER / PR: Negative
WT1: Negative
Ki-67: High (about 80%)
Mucicarmine: Focal luminal mucin only
Diagnostic Summary:
Specimen: Endobronchial (A) and transbronchial (B) biopsies, right lower lobe
Tumour present: Yes, in both A and B
Histological type: Adenocarcinoma, morphology of HPV-associated (usual-type) endocervical adenocarcinoma
Key immunoprofile: p16 block-positive; high-risk HPV RNA ISH positive; CK7+, CEA+; TTF-1−, Napsin A−; CK20−, CDX2 focal weak; ER/PR−, WT1−; PAX8−
Comparison with prior primary: Morphologically similar to the patient’s prior cervical adenocarcinoma (archival slides reviewed)
Primary site favoured: Uterine cervix (metastatic HPV-associated endocervical adenocarcinoma)
Primary lung adenocarcinoma: Not supported (TTF-1 and Napsin A negative; HPV ISH positive)
Further biomarkers: Not performed. PD-L1 or other markers can be done on request

Classification / standards used: Terminology per WHO Classification of Tumours, Female Genital Tumours, 5th edition (2020). A lung resection protocol is not applicable to a biopsy of metastatic tumour. All findings are illustrative sample data.

finalDiagnosis.label: A, B. Right lower lobe, endobronchial and transbronchial biopsies:
finalDiagnosis.text: Metastatic adenocarcinoma, consistent with metastasis from the patient’s known HPV-associated (usual-type) endocervical adenocarcinoma. p16 block-positive and high-risk HPV RNA in situ hybridisation positive. TTF-1 and Napsin A negative.

comment.text: The usual-type endocervical morphology is characterised by apical mitoses, apoptotic bodies and mucin-depleted cells with pseudostratified nuclei. The morphology resembles the prior cervical tumour, and the HPV-associated immunoprofile supports metastasis from the cervix rather than a new primary lung adenocarcinoma.

p16 alone is not specific: a proportion of primary lung adenocarcinomas, and other tumours, show strong p16 expression. Detection of high-risk HPV by RNA in situ hybridisation within the tumour cells is the decisive finding. Negative TTF-1 and Napsin A further argue against a lung primary, although a minority of lung adenocarcinomas (especially mucinous types) are negative for both. Negative CK20, CDX2 (only focal and weak), ER/PR and WT1 make metastases from the gastrointestinal tract, endometrium and ovary unlikely.

Molecular testing and PD-L1 immunohistochemistry are not routinely required for this diagnosis. They can be performed on the residual tissue on request, if needed to guide systemic therapy. Please correlate with imaging and the multidisciplinary team, including the absence of local pelvic recurrence.

containers.text: Endobronchial biopsies: Five tan-white, friable fragments, 1–4 mm.
Transbronchial biopsies: Four tan fragments, 1–2 mm, some floating.

exampleGross.sections: A1 endobronchial biopsies (entirely embedded); B1 transbronchial biopsies (entirely embedded). Three H&E levels on each block, with intervening unstained sections for IHC and in situ hybridisation.

micro.text: Sections show prostatic tissue with nodular hyperplasia (glandular and stromal nodules) and a striking, lobulocentric, mixed granulomatous inflammation:

Pattern: Granulomas centred on dilated and ruptured ducts and acini, with luminal debris, corpora amylacea and inspissated secretions. The inflammation spreads out from the ruptured glands into the stroma and replaces whole lobules in places. The lobular outlines are preserved at low power.

Cell types: Ill-formed and confluent granulomas made of epithelioid histiocytes with abundant pale-pink to foamy cytoplasm, and multinucleated (Langhans and foreign-body) giant cells. They are admixed with lymphocytes, many plasma cells, scattered eosinophils, and neutrophils that form small luminal microabscesses.
Necrosis: No caseating necrosis. No palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis.
Extent: Involves about 35% of the submitted tissue.

Negative findings: No Michaelis–Gutmann bodies or sheets of von Hansemann histiocytes. No sheets of lipid-laden foam cells beyond the focal foamy histiocytes (not xanthogranulomatous). No foreign material on polarisation. No organisms on H&E. No vasculitis.

The epithelium of the surviving glands shows reactive atypia. There is no high-grade PIN, no atypical glands suspicious for carcinoma, and no infiltrating single cells or cords. Immunohistochemistry confirms that the sheets of histiocytes are not carcinoma.
Special Stains / Immunohistochemistry:
Ziehl–Neelsen (A3, A5, A10): No acid-fast bacilli
Grocott (GMS) (A3, A5): No fungi
PAS / PAS-D (A3, A5): No fungi. No PAS-positive inclusions
Von Kossa / Perls (A5): No Michaelis–Gutmann bodies
Pancytokeratin AE1/AE3 (A3, A5): Negative in the histiocytes and giant cells; positive only in residual benign glands
PSA (A3): Negative in the histiocytic sheets; positive in the residual glandular epithelium
CD68 (A3): Strongly positive in epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells
p63 / HMWCK (A5): Basal cells present in the residual, reactive-looking glands

finalDiagnosis.label: A. Prostate, transurethral resection (22 g, entirely submitted):
finalDiagnosis.text: Nonspecific (idiopathic) granulomatous prostatitis, involving about 35% of the tissue, on a background of nodular hyperplasia. No caseation. ZN, GMS and PAS negative.
No high-grade PIN or carcinoma.

comment.text: Nonspecific granulomatous prostatitis is the most common form of granulomatous prostatitis. It is thought to be a reaction to secretions, bacterial toxins and cell debris leaking into the stroma from obstructed, ruptured ducts and acini, often after a urinary tract infection or bacterial prostatitis, as in this patient. It can produce a hard, nodular gland on DRE, a raised PSA and suspicious imaging, mimicking carcinoma clinically.
Differential diagnoses considered:

BCG-related granulomatous prostatitis: After intravesical BCG for bladder cancer. Discrete granulomas, often with caseating necrosis. Acid-fast bacilli are rarely seen. Excluded clinically here (no BCG history). Please confirm, as this history changes the interpretation.
Tuberculosis: Caseating granulomas. ZN negative and no caseation here.
Fungal infection: For example cryptococcosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis or histoplasmosis, especially in immunocompromised patients. GMS and PAS negative.
Post-biopsy / post-TURP granulomas: Palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis. Not seen, and no previous procedure.
Xanthogranulomatous prostatitis: Sheets of lipid-laden foam cells. Not the dominant pattern here.
Malakoplakia: Sheets of von Hansemann histiocytes with Michaelis–Gutmann bodies (von Kossa / Perls positive). Absent here.
Other: Systemic granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, allergic / eosinophilic prostatitis) and foreign-body reaction.

Sheets of epithelioid histiocytes can mimic high-grade (Gleason pattern 5) prostatic adenocarcinoma. Pancytokeratin and PSA are negative in the histiocytes, and CD68 is positive, which excludes carcinoma.

Clinical correlation is recommended. If an infectious cause remains a concern (for example immunosuppression, travel or occupational exposure, or BCG history), consider urine or tissue mycobacterial and fungal culture or PCR. PSA may stay raised for several months after inflammation, so follow-up PSA is advised before any further work-up for carcinoma.

containers.text: Prostatic chips (TURP): Multiple tan-white to yellow, rubbery and partly firm prostatic chips, 22 g in total, 0.3–1.6 cm. Several firm yellow chips are noted. No gritty or cheesy areas.

diagnoses.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Skin, Helix of Ear (Wide Local Excision)

micro.text: Sections show an invasive squamous cell carcinoma arising from atypical epidermis with full-thickness keratinocytic dysplasia and overlying ulceration and parakeratotic crust. The tumour is composed of irregular nests and cords of squamous cells with moderate nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, with focal keratin pearl formation and individual cell keratinisation. Greater than 75% of the tumour shows keratinisation (well differentiated). Tumour invades into the reticular dermis and superficial subcutis to a measured depth of 4.2 mm from the granular layer (Breslow-equivalent tumour thickness). No perineural invasion. No lymphovascular invasion. Host response shows a moderate chronic inflammatory infiltrate at the advancing edge. Peripheral margins (all clock faces) and the deep soft-tissue margin are free of tumour (closest peripheral 3.5 mm at 3 o'clock; deep 2.8 mm).

finalDiagnosis.label: Skin, left helix, wide local excision:
finalDiagnosis.text: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma, conventional type, well differentiated, 1.4 cm, thickness 4.2 mm, invading subcutis. No perineural or lymphovascular invasion. Margins negative. pT1 (AJCC 8th edition).

comment.text: High-risk features (ear site, thickness >4 mm, subcutis invasion) are noted. Clinical correlation for regional nodal assessment is advised as per institutional cutaneous SCC guidelines.

diagnoses.name: Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma, Classic Subtype (Total Thyroidectomy)

micro.text: Sections from the right lobe show an infiltrative, unencapsulated neoplasm composed of complex branching papillae with fibrovascular cores, admixed with neoplastic follicles. The lining cells show the diagnostic nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma: nuclear enlargement and elongation, overlapping, chromatin clearing (ground-glass nuclei), irregular nuclear membranes with grooves and intranuclear pseudoinclusions. Psammoma bodies and stromal fibrosis are present. Tall cells account for less than 30% of tumour cells; no hobnail, columnar or solid component is seen. No tumour necrosis; mitoses are inconspicuous. The tumour extends to, but does not breach, the thyroid capsule; no extrathyroidal extension. No lymphovascular invasion. All resection margins are free (closest posterior capsular margin 1.5 mm). Isthmus and left lobe show normal thyroid parenchyma with mild focal lymphocytic thyroiditis; no additional tumour foci. One of five level VI lymph nodes shows metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma (largest metastatic focus 0.3 cm) without extranodal extension; the remaining four nodes are reactive.

micro.text: Sections show a renal cell carcinoma with solid-alveolar and focally acinar architecture, separated by a delicate, richly branching ('chicken-wire') capillary network. Tumour cells have abundant clear cytoplasm with distinct cell membranes, and focal granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Nuclei are round with nucleoli conspicuous and eosinophilic at 400x magnification but inconspicuous at 100x (WHO/ISUP grade 2). No sarcomatoid or rhabdoid differentiation. No coagulative tumour necrosis. Areas of haemorrhage and small cysts with haemosiderin-laden macrophages are present. The tumour is surrounded by a fibrous pseudocapsule; there is no invasion of perinephric fat or renal sinus fat, and no involvement of the renal vein or its segmental branches. Renal vein, renal artery, ureteric and Gerota fascia margins are free of tumour. The adrenal gland is uninvolved. Non-neoplastic kidney shows mild arterionephrosclerosis with occasional globally sclerosed glomeruli (about 5%); no significant interstitial fibrosis.

The tumour bulges into but does not grossly penetrate the perinephric fat and is separated from the renal sinus by 0.8 cm of renal parenchyma. Remaining kidney shows a smooth cortex and unremarkable pelvicalyceal system. Adrenal gland is grossly unremarkable and separate from the tumour. No hilar lymph nodes identified.

exampleGross.sections: A1-A8: tumour (one block per cm) including tumour-perinephric fat interface and tumour-renal sinus interface; A9: renal vein and artery margins; A10: ureteric margin; A11: non-neoplastic kidney; A12: adrenal gland; A13: Gerota fascia margin.

diagnoses.name: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO Grade 4 (Temporal Lobe Resection)

micro.text: Sections show a diffusely infiltrating, highly cellular astrocytic glioma composed of pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic, irregular nuclei, scant to moderate fibrillary eosinophilic cytoplasm and occasional bizarre multinucleated giant cells. Mitotic figures are frequent, including atypical forms. There is florid microvascular proliferation with multilayered, glomeruloid vascular tufts, and extensive necrosis, including serpiginous necrosis with pseudopalisading of tumour cells. Tumour cells infiltrate the overlying cortex with perineuronal satellitosis and subpial accumulation (secondary structures of Scherer). Thrombosed vessels and haemorrhage are seen. No oligodendroglial, primitive neuronal or epithelioid component is identified.

Immunohistochemistry: GFAP: diffusely positive. OLIG2: positive in tumour nuclei. IDH1 R132H: negative. ATRX: retained nuclear expression. p53: positive in about 10% of tumour nuclei (wild-type pattern). H3 K27M: negative. Ki-67 (MIB-1) labelling index: about 35% in the most proliferative areas.

finalDiagnosis.label: Brain, right temporal lobe, resection:
finalDiagnosis.text: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4.

comment.text: Classification follows the WHO Classification of Central Nervous System Tumours. In a patient older than 55 years with a histologically classic, non-midline glioblastoma, absent IDH1 R132H staining and retained ATRX, IDH sequencing may be omitted. MGMT promoter methylation status is recommended for prognostic and treatment-planning purposes (temozolomide response), and will be issued as an addendum.

containers.text: Received multiple irregular fragments of soft, grey-tan to yellow brain tissue aggregating to 5.5 x 4.5 x 2.0 cm, with areas of yellow necrosis and haemorrhage. The largest fragment measures 3.8 x 2.5 x 1.8 cm. The tissue is submitted largely in toto, with representative cortical and necrotic areas separately sampled.

exampleGross.sections: A1: frozen section remnant; A2-A10: tumour including necrotic, cellular and cortical interface areas.

micro.text: Sections show acral-type skin, with a thick, compact stratum corneum, bearing an exophytic verrucous lesion:

Keratin layer: Marked compact orthohyperkeratosis with tiers of parakeratosis forming columns over the tips of the papillae (the 'church spire' pattern). Small collections of haemorrhage (red cells and haemosiderin) are trapped in the parakeratotic columns, corresponding to the clinical black dots.
Epidermis: Papillomatosis and acanthosis, with elongated rete ridges that curve inward towards the centre at the edges of the lesion (arborisation).
Granular layer: Thickened (hypergranulosis), with coarse, clumped keratohyaline granules in the valleys between the papillae.
Viral changes: Koilocytes in the upper spinous and granular layers: vacuolated cells with shrunken, hyperchromatic, raisinoid nuclei and a perinuclear halo.
Dermis: Dilated, tortuous capillaries in the elongated dermal papillae, some thrombosed. Mild superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.

Negative findings: No significant cytological atypia, atypical mitoses or dyskeratosis. No invasion: the base is a pushing, well-circumscribed interface. No large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (myrmecia pattern).
Margins: The lesion is completely excised. The deep margin is clear by 0.8 mm and the peripheral margins are clear by at least 1 mm.

finalDiagnosis.label: A. Skin, right thumb, shave excision:
finalDiagnosis.text: Verruca vulgaris (common viral wart). Completely excised; margins clear. No atypia or malignancy.

comment.text: The features are classic for verruca vulgaris, a benign epidermal proliferation caused by cutaneous human papillomavirus (HPV) types. They are papillomatosis, parakeratotic columns with trapped haemorrhage, hypergranulosis with coarse keratohyaline granules, koilocytes, inward-curving rete ridges and dilated papillary capillaries.
Differential diagnoses:

Clavus (corn) / callus: Compact hyperkeratosis on pressure sites. A clavus has a central keratin plug. Neither has papillomatosis, koilocytes, coarse keratohyaline granules or haemorrhagic parakeratotic columns, and skin lines are preserved over a callus.
Seborrhoeic keratosis: Rare on acral skin. It has horn pseudocysts and basaloid cells, without koilocytes or a thickened granular layer.

Verrucous carcinoma: A slow-growing, well-differentiated carcinoma (for example on the sole). It has bulbous, broad-based pushing invasion deep into the dermis and minimal atypia, so it needs adequate depth in sampling and clinical correlation. This small, superficial, well-circumscribed lesion shows no such features.
Myrmecia (deep palmoplantar wart): An endophytic wart with large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies. Not seen here.

HPV typing and p16 immunohistochemistry are not needed routinely for a common wart with typical morphology. Reserve them for atypical, persistent or periungual lesions where squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease) or invasive squamous cell carcinoma is a concern, especially in immunosuppressed patients. Warts can recur, because adjacent epidermis may harbour subclinical virus.

containers.text: Skin, right thumb: A grey-white, verrucous, hyperkeratotic shave of skin, 8 x 7 mm, 3 mm deep, with a papillary surface and small dark dots. The deep and peripheral margins are inked.

exampleGross.sections: A1 bisected (entirely embedded). Levels cut.

micro.text: Sections show a pure seminoma:
Tumour architecture: Sheets, nests and cords of uniform, polygonal tumour cells separated by delicate fibrous septa. The septa contain a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate.

Tumour cells: Abundant clear to pale-eosinophilic, glycogen-rich cytoplasm with well-defined cell borders. Central, squared-off round nuclei with granular chromatin and one or more prominent nucleoli. Frequent mitoses.
Granulomas: Scattered epithelioid granulomas within the septa.
Syncytiotrophoblastic cells: Rare isolated syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells, consistent with the mildly raised serum beta-hCG. No cytotrophoblasts or choriocarcinoma component.
Necrosis: Focal small areas of tumour necrosis, less than 5%.
Rete testis: The tumour shows pagetoid spread within the epithelium of the rete testis (A5), but there is no rete testis stromal invasion.
Lymphovascular invasion: Not identified in multiple sections, including at the hilum (A3, A5).
Extent: The tumour is confined to the testis. The tunica albuginea, tunica vaginalis, epididymis, hilar soft tissue and spermatic cord are not involved. The cord resection margin is free.
Non-seminomatous component: No embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, teratoma or choriocarcinoma component on morphology and IHC.

Background testis (A10–A11): Germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) in the adjacent seminiferous tubules. These are tubules lined by enlarged atypical germ cells with clear cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli along the basement membrane, OCT3/4 positive. The rest of the testis shows features typical of cryptorchidism: small atrophic tubules with thickened, hyalinised basement membranes, Sertoli-cell-only tubules with no spermatogenesis, and Leydig cell hyperplasia. A few microliths are present.
Immunohistochemistry:
OCT3/4: Diffuse strong nuclear positivity in tumour cells and in GCNIS
SALL4: Diffuse strong nuclear positivity
D2-40 (podoplanin): Membranous positivity
CD117 (c-KIT): Membranous positivity
CD30: Negative (excludes embryonal carcinoma)
AFP: Negative
Glypican-3: Negative (no yolk sac component)
Pancytokeratin AE1/AE3: Focal, weak dot-like positivity in a minority of cells
Beta-hCG: Positive only in the rare syncytiotrophoblastic cells
CD31 / D2-40 (vessels): No lymphovascular invasion confirmed

finalDiagnosis.label: A. Right testis (undescended) with spermatic cord, radical inguinal orchiectomy:
finalDiagnosis.text: Seminoma (pure), 2.6 cm, confined to the testis. No lymphovascular invasion. Pagetoid involvement of the rete testis without stromal invasion. Spermatic cord, epididymis and margin free of tumour. Germ cell neoplasia in situ in the adjacent tubules. Atrophic cryptorchid background. pT1a (AJCC 8th edition).

comment.text: Risk factors: the tumour is pure seminoma with no non-seminomatous component, confirmed by morphology and IHC (OCT3/4, SALL4, D2-40 and CD117 positive; CD30, AFP and glypican-3 negative). For stage I seminoma, the main pathological risk factors for occult metastatic relapse are tumour size more than 4 cm and rete testis stromal invasion. Neither is present here: the tumour is 2.6 cm, and the rete involvement is pagetoid only, without stromal invasion.

Marker and imaging correlation: rare syncytiotrophoblastic cells explain the mildly raised beta-hCG. Post-orchiectomy markers should be measured until they normalise. Final staging and management (surveillance or adjuvant therapy) depend on post-orchiectomy markers and imaging, and should be discussed at the multidisciplinary meeting.

Cryptorchidism association: cryptorchidism is a well-established risk factor for testicular germ cell tumours. The atrophy, hyalinised and Sertoli-cell-only tubules, microliths and GCNIS here are typical. The patient also has microlithiasis in the contralateral testis. Risk of a contralateral tumour is increased, so contralateral testis surveillance (self-examination and ultrasound as indicated) is advised. Fertility counselling and sperm banking should be considered before any further treatment.

containers.text: Right testis with spermatic cord (radical inguinal orchiectomy): Received fresh, then fixed after bivalving. A testis with epididymis and spermatic cord, 28 g. Testis 4.2 x 3.0 x 2.6 cm; spermatic cord 6.0 cm long, 1.2 cm in diameter. Tunica vaginalis intact and smooth; tunica albuginea smooth, without nodules, inked. Bivalving shows a well-circumscribed, lobulated, cream-tan, homogeneous, fleshy tumour, 2.6 x 2.2 x 2.0 cm, in the upper pole and centre, without haemorrhage, necrosis or cystic change. The tumour lies 2 mm from the tunica albuginea and does not breach it; it abuts the rete testis but does not grossly extend into the hilar soft tissue. Epididymis and spermatic cord grossly free. Residual testis small, pale and firm (atrophic).
